Evaluation, leakage, and reproducibility

Source: vignettes/evaluation-and-reproducibility.Rmd
evaluation-and-reproducibility.Rmd
library(graphlearnR)

A graph learning result is only as good as its evaluation. Graphs make it easy to leak test information into training, because examples are connected. This article collects the rules graphlearnR follows and the tools it gives you to report results that hold up.

Splits that do not leak

task splitter what it guarantees
node split_nodes() disjoint masks; stratified by class; unlabeled nodes excluded
edge label split_edge_labels() both directions of an undirected pair in the same split
link split_edges() held out pairs removed from the message passing graph; negatives are non edges of the full graph
heterogeneous link split_edges_hetero() held out edges also removed from the reverse relation
graph split_graphs() random, stratified, group (no group in two splits), or scaffold
temporal split_temporal() validation and test events are later than training events

Transductive node splits

In node classification on one graph, test nodes are present during training as unlabeled neighbors. That is the standard transductive setting and is not leakage, but two things would be:

  • computing feature normalization statistics on all nodes. Pass stats_mask = g$train_mask to normalize_features();
  • selecting a model or an epoch on test accuracy. Use the validation mask; train_graph_model() never looks at the test mask.
g <- split_nodes(dataset_sbm(c(40, 40, 40), seed = 1), seed = 1)
g <- normalize_features(g, stats_mask = g$train_mask)
round(colMeans(g$x[g$train_mask, ]), 10)[1:4]
#> [1] 0 0 0 0

Group and scaffold splits

When graphs come in related families (molecules sharing a scaffold, samples from the same patient), a random split puts near duplicates on both sides. Group splits keep each family in one split; scaffold splits put the largest families in training and the rare ones in the test set, which tests generalization to new structures.

families <- rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"), times = c(30, 20, 15, 10, 15, 10))
sp <- split_graphs(length(families), method = "group", groups = families, seed = 1)
lapply(sp, function(i) unique(families[i]))
#> $train
#> [1] "A" "D" "C" "F" "E"
#> 
#> $val
#> [1] "B"
#> 
#> $test
#> character(0)
sc <- split_graphs(length(families), method = "scaffold", groups = families)
lapply(sc, function(i) unique(families[i]))
#> $train
#> [1] "A" "B" "C" "E"
#> 
#> $val
#> [1] "D"
#> 
#> $test
#> [1] "F"

Metrics

evaluate_predictions() returns a tidy table for a task; the individual metrics are exported too.

truth <- factor(c("a", "a", "b", "b", "b", "c"))
prob <- rbind(c(0.7, 0.2, 0.1), c(0.4, 0.5, 0.1), c(0.1, 0.8, 0.1),
              c(0.2, 0.6, 0.2), c(0.3, 0.3, 0.4), c(0.1, 0.1, 0.8))
colnames(prob) <- levels(truth)
evaluate_predictions(truth, prob, "classification")
#>              metric     value
#> 1          accuracy 0.6666667
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 0.7222222
#> 3   precision_macro 0.7222222
#> 4      recall_macro 0.7222222
#> 5          f1_macro 0.6666667
#> 6               ece 0.3333333
#> 7             brier 0.3100000
#> 8           roc_auc 0.9629630
  • Classification: accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro precision, recall, and F1, one versus rest ROC AUC, Brier score, and expected calibration error.
  • Regression: MSE, RMSE, MAE, and R^2.
  • Links: ROC AUC, average precision, MRR, and Hits@k; with a negative matrix per positive, MRR and Hits@k rank each positive against its own negatives, and ties count half.
  • Clustering: normalized mutual information and adjusted Rand index.
c(nmi = metric_nmi(c(1, 1, 2, 2), c("x", "x", "y", "y")),
  ari = metric_ari(c(1, 1, 2, 2), c("x", "y", "x", "y")))
#>  nmi  ari 
#>  1.0 -0.5

Report variability

A single split and a single seed can mislead, especially on small graphs. Repeat over seeds and report a mean with a spread.

library(torch)
acc <- vapply(1:3, function(s) {
  gs <- split_nodes(dataset_sbm(c(40, 40, 40), feature_signal = 0.5, seed = 1), seed = s)
  torch_manual_seed(s)
  fit <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("sage", 8, 16, 3), gs, "node_classification",
                           epochs = 60, seed = s)
  ev <- evaluate_graph_model(fit, gs)
  ev$value[ev$metric == "accuracy"]
}, numeric(1))
c(mean = mean(acc), sd = sd(acc))
#>      mean        sd 
#> 0.9583333 0.0000000

Reproducibility

Every function that draws random numbers takes a seed and leaves the caller’s R random number stream untouched.

set.seed(123)
before <- .Random.seed
a <- sample_neighbors(dataset_karate(), 1:3, c(3, 3), seed = 9)
identical(.Random.seed, before)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(a$n_id, sample_neighbors(dataset_karate(), 1:3, c(3, 3), seed = 9)$n_id)
#> [1] TRUE

train_graph_model() seeds both R and torch. With the same seed, data, and model initialization, two CPU runs give the same losses. GPU kernels that use atomic additions (scatter sums) can differ in the last bits between runs.

run <- function() {
  torch_manual_seed(7)
  m <- gnn_model("gcn", 8, 16, 3)
  train_graph_model(m, g, "node_classification", epochs = 5, seed = 7)
}
f1 <- run()
f2 <- run()
identical(f1$history$train_loss, f2$history$train_loss)
#> [1] TRUE

Each fit stores what is needed to report or repeat it:

str(f1$reproducibility, max.level = 1)
#> List of 16
#>  $ seed           : num 7
#>  $ task           : chr "node_classification"
#>  $ hyperparameters:List of 6
#>  $ optimizer      : chr "adam"
#>  $ scheduler      : NULL
#>  $ loss           : chr "default"
#>  $ model_config   :List of 15
#>  $ model_class    : chr "graph_model"
#>  $ num_parameters : num 467
#>  $ dataset        :List of 7
#>  $ splits         : Named int [1:3] 72 24 24
#>   ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:3] "train" "val" "test"
#>  $ device         : chr "cpu"
#>  $ precision      : chr "float32"
#>  $ versions       : Named chr [1:3] "4.6.2" "0.1.0" "0.17.0"
#>   ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:3] "R" "graphlearnR" "torch"
#>  $ platform       : chr "x86_64-pc-linux-gnu"
#>  $ time           : chr "2026-11-13 11:29:25 UTC"

A checklist for papers and reports

  • State the split procedure, the split sizes, and whether the setting is transductive or inductive.
  • For link prediction, state how negatives were sampled and whether ranking metrics are filtered.
  • For temporal data, state the cut times and confirm no future events are used.
  • Report the mean and spread over at least three seeds, and a simple baseline (an MLP on features, a history baseline for dynamic links, the naive forecast for signals).
  • Record package versions and the device, as fit$reproducibility does.
